title: Part 2, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Which treats of the notable altercation Sancho Panza had with Don Quixote's niece and housekeeper, together with other droll matters

The history relates that the outcry Don Quixote, the curate, and the barber heard came from the niece and the housekeeper, who were shouting at Sancho — striving to bar the door against him as he tried to force his way in to see Don Quixote: "What does the vagabond want in this house? Be off to your own, brother, for it's you and no one else who deludes my master, and leads him astray, and takes him tramping about the country."

To which Sancho replied, "Devil's own housekeeper! It's I who am deluded, and led astray, and taken tramping about the country, not your master! He's carried me all over the world, and you're greatly mistaken. He enticed me away from home by a trick, promising me an island that I'm still waiting for."
"May evil islands choke you, you detestable Sancho," said the niece. "What are islands? Is it something to eat, glutton and gormandiser that you are?"
"It's not something to eat," replied Sancho, "but something to govern and rule — and better than four cities or four judgeships at court."
"For all that," said the housekeeper, "you don't come in here, you bag of mischief and sack of knavery; go govern your house and dig your seed-patch, and give over looking for islands or shy-lands."

The curate and the barber listened with great amusement to the words of the three; but Don Quixote, anxious lest Sancho blab and blurt out a whole heap of mischievous stupidities — touching on points that might not be altogether to his credit — called to him and made the other two hold their tongues and let him in. Sancho entered, and the curate and the barber took their leave of Don Quixote, of whose recovery they despaired when they saw how wedded he was to his crazy ideas and how saturated with the nonsense of his unlucky chivalry. Said the curate to the barber, "You'll see, gossip, that when we are least thinking of it, our gentleman will be off once more for another flight."

"I have no doubt of it," returned the barber; "but I don't wonder so much at the madness of the knight as at the simplicity of the squire, who has such a firm belief in all that about the island that I suppose no amount of exposure imaginable would get it out of his head."

"God help them," said the curate; "and let us be on the lookout to see what comes of all these absurdities of the knight and squire — for it seems as if they had both been cast in the same mould, and the madness of the master without the simplicity of the man would not be worth a farthing."
"That's true," said the barber, "and I would very much like to know what the pair are talking about at this moment."
"I promise you," said the curate, "the niece or the housekeeper will tell us by and by, for they're not the ones to forget to listen."

Meanwhile Don Quixote shut himself up in his room with Sancho, and when they were alone he said to him, "It grieves me greatly, Sancho, that you should have said, and still say, that I took you out of your cottage, when you know I did not stay in my own house. We sallied forth together, took the road together, wandered abroad together; we have had the same fortune and the same luck; if they blanketed you once, they belaboured me a hundred times, and that's the only advantage I have over you."
"That was only reasonable," replied Sancho, "for, by what your worship says, misfortunes belong more properly to knights-errant than to their squires."
"You are mistaken, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "according to the maxim _quando caput dolet_, etc."
"I don't understand any language but my own," said Sancho.

"I mean to say," said Don Quixote, "that when the head suffers, all the members suffer; and so, being your lord and master, I am your head, and you, being my servant, are a part of me; therefore any evil that affects, or shall affect, me should give you pain, and what affects you should give pain to me."

"It should be so," said Sancho, "but when I was blanketed as a member, my head was on the other side of the wall, looking on while I was flying through the air, and felt no pain whatever; and if the members are obliged to feel the suffering of the head, then the head should be obliged to feel theirs."

"Do you mean to say now, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that I felt nothing while they were blanketing you? If you do, you must not say so or think it, for I felt more pain then in spirit than you did in body. But let us put that aside for the present, for we shall have opportunities enough to consider and settle the point. Tell me, Sancho my friend, what do they say about me here in the village? What do the common people think of me? What do the hidalgos? What do the caballeros? What do they say of my valour; of my achievements; of my courtesy? How do they treat the task I have undertaken in reviving and restoring to the world the now forgotten order of chivalry? In short, Sancho, I would have you tell me everything that has come to your ears on this subject — and you are to tell me without adding anything to the good or taking anything from the bad; for it is the duty of loyal vassals to tell the truth to their lords just as it is and in its proper shape, neither letting flattery add to it nor any idle deference lessen it. And I would have you know, Sancho, that if the naked truth, undisguised by flattery, reached the ears of princes, times would be different, and other ages would be reckoned iron ages more than ours — which I hold to be the golden age of these latter days. Take the benefit of this advice, Sancho, and report to me clearly and faithfully the truth of what you know touching what I have asked of you."

"That I'll do with all my heart, master," replied Sancho, "provided your worship will not be vexed at what I say, since you wish me to say it out in all its nakedness, without putting any more clothes on it than it came to my knowledge in."
"I will not be vexed at all," returned Don Quixote; "you may speak freely, Sancho, without beating about the bush."

"Well then," he said, "first of all I have to tell you that the common people take your worship for a mighty great madman, and me for no less a fool. The hidalgos say that, not keeping within the bounds of your quality of gentleman, you've assumed the 'Don,' and made a knight of yourself at a jump, with four vine-stocks and a couple of acres of land and never a shirt to your back. The caballeros say they don't want to have hidalgos setting up in opposition to them, particularly squire hidalgos who polish their own shoes and darn their black stockings with green silk."
"That," said Don Quixote, "does not apply to me, for I always go well dressed and never patched; ragged I may be, but ragged more from the wear and tear of arms than of time."

"As to your worship's valour, courtesy, accomplishments, and task, there's a variety of opinions. Some say 'mad but droll'; others, 'valiant but unlucky'; others, 'courteous but meddling' — and then they go into such a number of things that they don't leave a whole bone in either your worship or myself."

"Recollect, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that wherever virtue exists in any eminent degree, it is persecuted. Few or none of the famous men who have lived escaped being calumniated by malice. Julius Caesar, the boldest, wisest, and bravest of captains, was charged with being ambitious, and not particularly clean in his dress, or pure in his morals. Of Alexander, whose deeds won him the name of Great, they say he was something of a drunkard. Of Hercules, him of the many labours, it is said he was lewd and luxurious. Of Don Galaor, the brother of Amadis of Gaul, it was whispered that he was over-quarrelsome, and of his brother that he was lachrymose. So, O Sancho, amid all these calumnies against good men, mine may be let pass, since they are no more than what you have said."
"That's just where it is, body of my father!"
"Is there more, then?" asked Don Quixote.

"There's the tail to be skinned yet," said Sancho; "all so far is cakes and fancy bread. But if your worship wants to know all about the calumnies they bring against you, I'll fetch you one this instant who can tell you the whole of them without missing an atom; for last night the son of Bartholomew Carrasco, who has been studying at Salamanca, came home after being made a bachelor, and when I went to welcome him, he told me your worship's history is already abroad in books, with the title of THE INGENIOUS GENTLEMAN DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA. And he says they mention me in it by my own name of Sancho Panza, and the lady Dulcinea del Toboso too, and various things that happened to us when we were alone — so much so that I crossed myself in wonder at how the historian who wrote them down could have known them."
"I promise you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "the author of our history will be some sage enchanter; for to such, nothing they choose to write about is hidden."
"What!" said Sancho. "A sage and an enchanter! Why, the bachelor Samson Carrasco (that's the name of him I spoke of) says the author of the history is called Cide Hamete Berengena."
"That is a Moorish name," said Don Quixote.
"Maybe so," replied Sancho; "for I have heard say that the Moors are mostly great lovers of berengenas."
"You must have mistaken the surname of this 'Cide' — which means in Arabic 'Lord,' Sancho," observed Don Quixote.
"Very likely," replied Sancho, "but if your worship wishes me to fetch the bachelor, I'll go for him in a twinkling."
"You will do me a great pleasure, my friend," said Don Quixote, "for what you have told me has amazed me, and I shall not eat a morsel that will agree with me until I've heard all about it."
"Then I'm off for him," said Sancho; and leaving his master, he went in search of the bachelor, with whom he returned in a short time; and the three of them together had a very droll conversation.
